messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node RL from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (vavg)
        *   $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (vmax)
        *   $Ripple \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (vpp)
        *   $Startup \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (tup)
        *   $Settled \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (dv)
    *   Piezo Model: $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and 20 M$\Omega$ leakage.
    *   Operating Conditions: S1 (Nominal), S2 (Heavy Load), S3 (Strong Excitation/Light Load), S4 (Weak Excitation), S5 (Low Freq), S6 (Hot/Cp+20%).
    *   Voltage constraints are tight: $1.8\text{ V} \le V_{out} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.
    *   Reference (FBR):
        *   S2: $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{ V}$ (FAIL - too low)
        *   S3: $V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V}$ (FAIL - too high)
        *   S4: $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{ V}$ (FAIL - too low)
        *   S5: $dv$ FAIL (not settled)

    *   $V_{oc} \approx \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p}$. For S1: $\frac{50\mu\text{A}}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 3.18\text{ V}$.
    *   With a full bridge, the voltage at the storage capacitor is roughly $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} - 2V_D$. For $V_D \approx 0.25\text{ V}$, $V_{out} \approx 2.68\text{ V}$.
    *   S4 (Weak Excitation): $I_p = 30\mu\text{A}$. $V_{oc} \approx 1.9\text{ V}$. $V_{out} \approx 1.9 - 0.5 = 1.4\text{ V}$. (Explains FBR failure).
    *   S3 (Strong Excitation): $I_p = 100\mu\text{A}$. $V_{oc} \approx 6.37\text{ V}$. $V_{out} \approx 6.37 - 0.5 = 5.87\text{ V}$. (Explains FBR failure).

    *   To improve efficiency and boost voltage for S4/S2, we need something better than a bridge.
    *   Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE) or Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) are standard.
    *   SSHI: Uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks. This increases the average voltage delivered to the rectifier.
    *   SECE: Uses an inductor to extract the charge from $C_p$ more efficiently.
    *   Let's consider a modified SSHI or an active rectifier. Since we only have `SYNC` controllers and switches, a synchronous inverter (SSHI) combined with a rectifier or a simplified charge pump is feasible.

    *   *Design 1: SSHI-like Inverter with Bridge.*
        An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ across the piezo to invert $V_{Cp}$. This increases the voltage swing.
        Connectivity: Piezo $\to$ Bridge $\to$ Out. Switch $S$ and $L$ in parallel with piezo to flip polarity.
        Actually, a simpler SSHI approach: the switch $S$ and inductor $L$ are in series across the piezo. When $V_{pzp}$ reaches peak, $S$ closes, $L$ resonates with $C_p$ to flip the voltage.

    *   *Design 2: Zener Clamp.*
        S3 fails because $V_{max} > 3.6\text{ V}$. A Zener diode (DZ33) on the output can clamp the voltage to 3.3 V.

    *   *Design 3: Active Rectification (if possible).*
        We only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs. A full bridge of switches is 4 switches. But SYNCs are limited to 2.
        A half-wave synchronous rectifier? Or a bridge of diodes with an SSHI stage.

    *   **Topology A: SSHI + FBR + Zener Clamp.**
        SSHI improves the voltage for S2/S4.
        Zener clamp prevents S3 from overvoltage.
        FBR ensures rectification.
        Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ across the piezo.

        Wait, SSHI typically works by flipping the voltage of $C_p$ relative to the rectifier.
        Standard SSHI: $L$ and $S$ in series, connected across $pzp$ and $pzn$.
        $S$ closes at $V_{max}$ and $V_{min}$ (edges="both").
        $T_{on} \approx \frac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{L C_p}$ (for a half-cycle flip) or $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$ depending on the circuit. The prompt says $T_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.

    *   **Topology B: SECE-like approach (Parallel SSHI).**
        Instead of a bridge, use a synchronous switch to dump $C_p$ energy into the storage capacitor.
        Since we have limited switches, let's try a "Synchronous Switch" that connects $pzp$ to `out` via an inductor.

    *   **Topology C: Simple Bridge + Zener (The Baseline Improvement).**
        Just adding a Zener to the FBR. It solves S3, but not S2/S4.

    *   Let's refine Topology A (SSHI + FBR + Zener).
        1.  Inductor $L1$ from $pzp$ to $n1$.
        2.  Switch $S1$ from $n1$ to $pzn$.
        3.  SYNC $G1$ controls $S1$, edges="both".
        4.  FBR: $D1[pzp, out]$, $D2[pzn, out]$, $D3[0, pzp]$, $D4[0, pzn]$. (Wait, this is a full bridge. $D3, D4$ are return diodes).
        5.  Zener $DZ1[0, out]$.
        6.  Capacitor $C_{out}[out, 0]$.

        Check: Does $S1$ and $L1$ flip the voltage?
        When $V_{pzp}$ is max, $S1$ closes. $L1$ and $C_p$ form a resonant circuit. $V_{pzp}$ flips to $-V_{pzp}$.
        This effectively increases the available voltage for the bridge.

    *   Let's reconsider the FBR connectivity:
        Standard Bridge:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        Wait, the prompt says: "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have their anode on ground)". This matches.

    *   Let's try to be more efficient. An SSHI with a bridge is good.
        What about a "Synchronous Rectifier" using switches?
        S1: pzp -> out
        S2: pzn -> out
        But we only have 2 SYNCs. We could have one SYNC for $S1$ (edges="pos") and one for $S2$ (edges="neg").
        But we still need the return path to ground. Without diodes, we need 2 more switches for the return path. That's 4 switches.
        Sync 1: closes S1 (pzp->out) and S3 (0->pzn) at positive peak? No, SYNC is linked to the piezo.
        If SYNC1 handles "pos" and SYNC2 handles "neg", and each SYNC can control multiple switches? The prompt says `ctrl: id of a SYNC`. So yes, multiple switches can share one SYNC.

        *Synchronous Bridge:*
        S1: pzp -> out (ctrl: G1, edges: "pos")
        S2: 0 -> pzn (ctrl: G1, edges: "pos")
        S3: pzn -> out (ctrl: G2, edges: "neg")
        S4: 0 -> pzp (ctrl: G2, edges: "neg")
        This is a synchronous bridge. It removes the diode drop ($\sim 0.5\text{V}$), which would significantly help S2 and S4.

    *   Now, combine Synchronous Bridge + Zener Clamp.
        Wait, I can also add an SSHI stage to the Synchronous Bridge.
        SSHI: $L1$ and $S5$ across $pzp-pzn$. (But we only have 4 switches max).
        If I use 4 switches for the bridge, I can't use one for SSHI.
        If I use 2 diodes for the return path and 2 switches for the forward path?
        D1: 0 -> pzp
        D2: 0 -> pzn
        S1: pzp -> out (ctrl: G1, edges: "pos")
        S2: pzn -> out (ctrl: G2, edges: "neg")
        This uses 2 switches and 2 diodes. I have 2 switches left.
        One switch $S3$ and inductor $L1$ for SSHI.

    *   **Refining Topology 1: Synchronous-assisted Bridge + Zener.**
        S1: pzp -> out (ctrl: G1, edges: "pos")
        S2: pzn -> out (ctrl: G2, edges: "neg")
        D1: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        D2: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
        C1: out -> 0 (Storage)
        DZ1: 0 -> out (Zener)
        This removes one diode drop.

    *   **Refining Topology 2: SSHI + FBR + Zener.**
        D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
        D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
        D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1, edges: "both")
        C1: out -> 0
        DZ1: 0 -> out (Zener)
        This increases the voltage swing.

    *   **Refining Topology 3: Synchronous-assisted Bridge + SSHI + Zener.**
        S1: pzp -> out (ctrl: G1, edges: "pos")
        S2: pzn -> out (ctrl: G2, edges: "neg")
        D1: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        D2: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S3: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1, edges: "both") -- Wait, G1 is "pos", S3 needs "both".
        Let's use G1 for the SSHI and G2 for the bridge? No, we need G1 and G2 for the two halves of the bridge.
        Maybe the SSHI doesn't need a separate SYNC? If G1 is "pos" and G2 is "neg", we can't easily do "both" for the SSHI unless we use a third SYNC (but we only have 2).
        Wait, we can use G1 for the "pos" side of the bridge and the "pos" part of the SSHI, and G2 for the "neg" side of the bridge and the "neg" part of the SSHI.
        S1: pzp -> out (ctrl: G1, edges: "pos")
        S3: pzp -> n1 (No, this is wrong)
        Let's use a simpler SSHI: $L1$ and $S3$ across the piezo, $S3$ controlled by $G1$ (edges: "pos"). This only flips the voltage once per cycle. Not ideal.

    *   Let's focus on the most promising:
        1.  FBR + Zener + SSHI (G1 edges="both").
        2.  Synchronous-assisted Bridge (S1-pos, S2-neg, D1, D2) + Zener.
        3.  Full Synchronous Bridge (S1-pos, S2-pos, S3-neg, S4-neg) + Zener.
            S1: pzp -> out (G1, pos)
            S2: 0 -> pzn (G1, pos)
            S3: pzn -> out (G2, neg)
            S4: 0 -> pzp (G2, neg)
            C1: out -> 0
            DZ1: 0 -> out (Zener)

    *   *Comparison:*
        - Full Sync Bridge: Best for S2/S4 (zero diode drop). $V_{out}$ will be higher.
        - FBR + SSHI: Best for S2/S4 (voltage boosting).
        - Full Sync Bridge + Zener: Solves S3 (Zener) and S2/S4 (Sync).

    *   Let's evaluate the Full Sync Bridge + Zener further.
        S1, S2 (G1, pos); S3, S4 (G2, neg).
        S1: pzp -> out
        S2: 0 -> pzn
        S3: pzn -> out
        S4: 0 -> pzp
        This is essentially a bridge where the diodes are replaced by switches.
        The power cost of 2 SYNCs is $0.5\mu\text{A} \cdot 2 = 1\mu\text{A}$.
        At 1.8 V, this is $1.8\mu\text{W}$.
        The load power for S4 is $1.8^2 / 1000\text{k} \approx 3.2\mu\text{W}$.
        Total power needed $\approx 5\mu\text{W}$.
        S4 piezo power: $P_{avg} \approx \frac{I_p^2}{2 \cdot 2\pi f C_p} \cdot \eta \approx \frac{(30\mu\text{A})^2}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx \frac{900 \cdot 10^{-12}}{1.57 \cdot 10^{-5}} \approx 57\mu\text{W}$.
        So a Synchronous Bridge is very efficient and should easily cover S4.

    *   What about S3? $V_{oc} \approx 6.37\text{V}$. Without a Zener, $V_{out}$ will rise to $6.37\text{V}$. The limit is $3.6\text{V}$.
        A Zener DZ33 (3.3 V) will clamp it.

    *   Is there any risk? The switches $S1 \dots S4$ are ideal ($R_{on} = 2\Omega$).
        The "settled" condition ($dv < 0.02\text{V}$) and "ripple" ($vpp < 0.05\text{V}$) depend on the storage capacitor $C_{out}$.
        For S3 (light load $2.2\text{M}\Omega$), $C_{out}$ should be large enough to keep ripple low.
        For S2 (heavy load $150\text{k}\Omega$), $C_{out}$ should be large enough to maintain $V_{out} > 1.8\text{V}$.

    *   *Wait, one detail:* The SYNC controller closes switches for `ton` seconds *at the piezo voltage extrema*.
        In a standard bridge, we want the switches to be closed for the *entire half-period*.
        But `ton` is limited to $0.001\text{s}$ (1 ms).
        At $f=100\text{Hz}$, the half-period is $5\text{ms}$.
        So `ton` cannot cover the whole half-period.
        This means the "Synchronous Bridge" using `SYNC` is actually a *switched-capacitor* type of rectifier, not a continuous one.
        If $t_{on} = 1\text{ms}$ and $T/2 = 5\text{ms}$, we only collect charge for 20% of the time.
        This might be worse than a diode bridge!

    *   *Rethink:* Diode bridges conduct as long as $V_{piezo} > V_{out} + V_D$.
        If we use `SYNC` for rectification, we only get a pulse of current.
        This is exactly what SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction) does.
        In SECE, you use an inductor to quickly move the charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.

    *   *SECE Topology:*
        $L1$ from $pzp$ to $n1$, $S1$ from $n1$ to $out$.
        When $V_{pzp}$ is max, $S1$ closes, $L1$ transfers charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
        Wait, the standard SECE is: $S1$ connects $pzp$ to $L1$, and $L1$ is connected to $C_{out}$ through another switch or diode.
        Actually, the simplest SECE-like circuit:
        $L1$ and $S1$ in series from $pzp$ to $out$.
        $S1$ closes at $V_{max}$ (edges="pos").
        Wait, this only works if $V_{pzp}$ is significantly higher than $V_{out}$.
        If $V_{out}$ is $1.8\text{V}$ and $V_{pzp}$ is $3.2\text{V}$, it works.
        But we also need to extract charge from the negative peak.
        $L2$ and $S2$ in series from $pzn$ to $out$.
        $S2$ closes at $V_{min}$ (edges="neg").

    *   *Let's try this "Dual-Inductor SECE":*
